title: Grouping numbers into ranges with pd.cut
setup:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("players.csv")
explanation: Back to the players. Often you want categories instead of raw numbers, like Casual, Regular and Hardcore players. pd.cut() sorts numbers into ranges called bins. bins=[0, 100, 300, 1000] makes three ranges: over 0 up to 100, over 100 up to 300, and over 300 up to 1000. Each range includes its top number. labels names each range, in order. It's the pandas version of CASE WHEN in SQL.

tasks.prompt: Predict first: how many players will be Regular (over 100, up to 300 hours)?

solution_lines.explain: Regular is over 100 and up to 300: 4 players.

tasks.prompt: Fill in the blank so Regular means over 100 and up to 300 hours.
hints: The bins list holds the edges of the ranges, in order.

solution_lines.explain: Edges at 0, 100, 300 and 1000 make three ranges.

tasks.prompt: Add a level column using pd.cut (Casual, Regular, Hardcore, with the bins from the example), then show username and level.
hints: Same as the example, but show two columns.
df["level"] = pd.cut(df["hours_played"], bins=[0, 100, 300, 1000], labels=["Casual", "Regular", "Hardcore"]), then df[["username", "level"]]

tasks.prompt: Count the players in each level, in the order Casual, Regular, Hardcore.
hints: value_counts() sorts by count. sort_index() puts them back in label order.

tasks.prompt: Add the level column, then show the average hours per level, rounded to 1 decimal.
hints: Make the column, then groupby it. Add observed=True inside groupby() for category columns, to avoid a warning.

recap: You just learned to turn numbers into categories with pd.cut(bins=..., labels=...), then count and summarise each category.
